{{italic title}}
'''''The Secrets of Triangles: A Mathematical Journey''''' is a [[popular mathematics]] book on the [[geometry]] of [[triangle]]s. It was written by [[Alfred S. Posamentier]] and {{ill|Ingmar Lehmann|de}}, and published in 2012 by [[Prometheus Books]].

==Topics==
The book consists of ten chapters,{{r|leversha}} with the first six concentrating on [[triangle center]]s while the final four cover more diverse topics including the [[area]] of triangles, [[Inequality (mathematics)|inequalities]] involving triangles, [[straightedge and compass construction]]s, and [[fractal]]s.{{r|mcandrew}}

Beyond the classical triangle centers (the [[circumcenter]], [[incenter]], [[orthocenter]], and [[centroid]]) the book covers other centers including the [[Brocard points]], [[Fermat point]], [[Gergonne point]], and other geometric objects associated with triangle centers such as the [[Euler line]], [[Simson line]], and [[nine-point circle]].{{r|leversha}}

The chapter on areas includes both [[trigonometry|trigonometric]] formulas and [[Heron's formula]] for computing the area of a triangle from its side lengths, and the chapter on inequalities includes the [[Erdős–Mordell inequality]] on sums of distances from the sides of a triangle and [[Weitzenböck's inequality]] relating the area of a triangle to that of squares on its sides.{{r|mcandrew}}
Under constructions, the book considers 95 different triples of elements from which a triangle's shape may be determined (taken from its side lengths, angles, medians, heights, or angle bisectors) and describes how to find a triangle with each combination for which this is possible.{{r|vdv}} Triangle-related fractals in the final chapter include the [[Sierpiński triangle]] and [[Koch snowflake]].{{r|mcandrew}}

==Audience and reception==
Reviewer Alasdair McAndrew criticizes the book as being too "breathless" in its praise of the geometry it discusses and too superficial to be of interest to professional mathematicians,{{r|mcandrew}} and Patricia Baggett writes that little of its content would be of use in high school mathematics education. However, Baggett suggests that it may be usable as a reference work,{{r|baggett}} and similarly Robert Dawson suggests using its chapter on inequalities in this way.{{r|dawson}} The book is written at a level suitable for high school students and interested amateurs,{{r|leversha|vdv}} and McAndrew recommends the book to them.{{r|mcandrew}}

Both Baggett and Gerry Leversha find the chapter on fractals (written by Robert A. Chaffer){{r|bumcrot}} to be the weakest part of the book,{{r|leversha|baggett}} and Joop van der Vaart calls this chapter interesting but not a good fit for the rest of the book.{{r|vdv}} Leversha calls the chapter on area "a bit of a mish-mash". Otherwise, Baggett evaluates the book as "well written and well illustrated", although lacking a glossary.{{r|baggett}} Robert Dawson calls the book "very readable", and recommends it to any mathematics library.{{r|dawson}}
